title: Kunti's half for Bhima
hookLine: in hiding, a mother splits the begged food in two, half for one son: the Gita's middle way of eating
carry: yukta: eat in measure, by your own fire
tomorrow: who is eating when you eat?
last: DO NOT SPEAK ILL OF FOOD.

cards: The five Pandava brothers are in hiding, dressed as poor brahmins, living on what they can beg in a small town called Ekachakra. Every evening they bring the food home to their mother, Kunti, and she divides it.
Not in six equal shares. She splits it in two. Half goes to one son, Bhima.
The other half she shares among the rest of them and herself. It sounds unfair, until you meet Bhima. Today, the measure.

teach.b: Bhima is the strongest of the brothers, and the Mahabharata gives him a nickname, Vrikodara, wolf-belly, for his enormous hunger. Kunti isn't playing favorites. She's feeding each son by what he needs.
Ayurveda has a word for that: matra, measure.

teach.h: MATRA: MEASURE BY YOUR OWN FIRE
teach.b: Charaka's chapter on the daily round begins, paraphrased: one should eat in measure, and the measure depends on the strength of your own digestive fire. Bhima's fire is huge. Yours may not be.
Charaka even gives a picture: fill the stomach's room in three parts, one with food, one with drink, and leave one for the body's own workings. Don't fill it to the top.

Now the Hindu teaching that makes this more than a diet. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna, paraphrased, that yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all.
It's for the one who is yukta, measured, balanced, in eating and rest, in sleeping and waking, in work. For that person, he says, yoga ends sorrow. Notice both edges are ruled out.

teach.h: NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE
teach.b: Stuffing yourself is out, and so is starving yourself to look holy.

That's why Hindu fasts, at their best, are kept with care, often with fruit and milk, and why a grandmother keeping Ekadashi will still make sure you eat. The measure isn't a number handed down from outside.
It's yours, and finding it is part of the spiritual path, as Kunti knew when she gave Bhima half.

how: People who follow Ayurveda eat in measure, the amount their own digestion handles well, leaving some room rather than eating until full; many Hindus keep fasts such as Ekadashi with fruit and milk, in the spirit of the Gita's measured eating.

o: measure by your own fire: the Gita's middle way of eating
one fixed portion that suits everyone the same
fasting hardest as the surest sign of holiness

p: measure, set by your own fire
the third part of the stomach
left for the body's own workings

s: Kunti split the food into equal shares for everyone
she gave Bhima half, by his need, and shared the rest.
the Gita says yoga is not for one who eats too much or not at all
it's for the one who is measured in eating, sleeping and waking, work and rest.
Charaka gives one fixed portion size for everyone
the measure depends on the strength of each person's digestive fire.

games.q: you're Kunti, with one bowl of alms and six mouths. what do you do?
o: split it by need: half for Bhima, the rest shared.
six equal portions, no matter who is hungrier.
skip your own share to look more devoted.
games.why: Kunti feeds each by his fire, like Charaka's measure. and the Gita rules out both edges: too much, and nothing at all.

practice: Rest a hand on your stomach if you like, and ask quietly: empty, part-full, or full? Answer with what's there, not with a judgment, and feel the breath moving under your hand.
If you pray, offer the next meal before it comes, as many Hindus do. If you don't, simply promise to notice when it's enough.

wordCard.voice: Food as practice. Matra and yukta: measure set by your own fire, and the Gita's middle way, neither too much nor too little. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: yukta, joined, balanced. In Gita 6.17, the yogi measured in eating, rest and work.

carryVoice: Your line: yukta, eat in measure, by your own fire, the way Kunti gave Bhima half. Go gently.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, the Pandavas at Ekachakra (Kunti divides the begged food, half to Bhima and half among the rest); Bhima called Vrikodara
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 5 (one should eat in measure; the measure depends on the strength of the digestive fire)
Charaka Samhita, Vimanasthana 2 (the stomach in three parts: solid food, liquids, and space for the doshas)
Bhagavad Gita 6.16–17 (yoga is not for one who eats too much or not at all; for one measured in food, recreation, work, sleep and waking, yoga destroys sorrow)
